learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics: Solar as Architecture
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics replaces conventional building materials with solar-generating surfaces, turning windows, facades, and rooftops into power plants. As cities account for 70% of global CO2 emissions, BIPV offers a powerful path to decarbonize the built environment while preserving architectural beauty and generating clean electricity on-site.
learn.c1_text: Unlike rooftop solar panels bolted onto finished buildings, BIPV materials ARE the building envelope. Solar shingles serve as roofing; photovoltaic glass forms curtain walls and skylights; spandrel panels clad facades. Each element performs a dual function—structural and electrical—saving material costs while generating power exactly where energy is consumed.
learn.c2_text: Building-applied retrofits (like Tesla Solar Roof) sit atop existing surfaces, while building-integrated systems embed directly into the structure during construction. Thin-film technologies excel here because they allow partial light transmission, enabling tinted windows that still produce electricity. Efficiency ranges 8-15%, lower than rigid panels but acceptable when offset by aesthetic and material savings.
learn.c3_text: India's building stock is projected to double by 2030, with the National Solar Mission encouraging net-zero buildings through ECBC codes. Indian architects increasingly specify BIPV for IT parks in Bengaluru and green-certified offices in Hyderabad, where space constraints and aesthetic demands favor integrated solar over rooftop arrays.

learn.stat2: BIPV can reduce a building's energy consumption by 50-70%
learn.stat3: India aims for net-zero buildings in major commercial complexes by 2030
learn.stat4: Photovoltaic glass transmits 10-50% of light while generating electricity

learn.title: Floating Offshore Wind: Deep Water Power
learn.intro: Floating offshore wind platforms unlock wind resources in waters deeper than 60 meters, where traditional fixed-bottom turbines cannot be installed. Over 80% of global offshore wind potential lies in deep waters, making floating platforms essential for scaling offshore wind beyond near-shore limits and reaching coastal nations with steep continental shelves.
learn.c1_text: Three main concepts anchor floating turbines to the seabed. Semi-submersibles use buoyancy columns with ballast; spar buoys are long cylinders extending deep underwater; tension-leg platforms (TLPs) use taut vertical mooring lines. Each design balances stability, cost, and water depth, with spar buoys currently dominating demonstration projects.
learn.c2_text: Traditional monopile foundations become uneconomical beyond 50-60 meters water depth due to immense steel requirements. Floating platforms decouple the turbine from the seabed, using chains or tethers to maintain position. This lets developers access richer, steadier winds 100+ km offshore, where capacity factors can exceed 60%.
learn.c3_text: India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy targets 30 GW of offshore capacity, largely off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu coasts where seabed drops sharply. The National Institute of Wind Energy has identified sites with 200+ GW potential at depths exceeding 50 meters, where only floating platforms can harness this resource.
learn.stat1: A single 15 MW floating turbine can power 19,000 homes annually
learn.stat2: Floating offshore wind costs have fallen from ~USD 200/MWh (2015) to under USD 100/MWh by 2030 projections
learn.stat3: Global floating wind capacity is projected to reach 380 GW by 2050
learn.stat4: Capacity factors for floating wind average 55-65%, versus 25-45% for onshore

learn.title: India's PLI Scheme for Solar Manufacturing
learn.intro: India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for solar manufacturing aims to reduce import dependence—particularly from China—and build a self-reliant domestic solar supply chain. With solar capacity targets of 500 GW by 2030, indigenous module and cell manufacturing is critical for energy security, jobs, and lowering project costs through domestic competition.
learn.c1_text: The INR 19,500 crore (USD 2.4 billion) PLI scheme rewards manufacturers based on incremental sales of high-efficiency solar modules and cells. Companies receive per-megawatt subsidies for actual production, not promised capacity, ensuring taxpayer money funds real output. Performance-linked incentives (separate from PLI) further reward higher-efficiency TOPCon and HJT cells.
learn.c2_text: The scheme promotes vertical integration from polysilicon to modules. Earlier policies subsidized only final assembly, leaving India dependent on imported wafers. New tranches mandate backward integration, encouraging Indian players to manufacture wafers, cells, and modules domestically, creating complete supply chains resilient to geopolitical disruptions.
learn.c3_text: Adani, Reliance, Tata, and Waaree have committed over 100 GW of integrated manufacturing capacity under the PLI. By 2026, India aims to manufacture 100+ GW of solar modules domestically, reducing imports from 80% (2022) toward 30%. This translates into roughly 100,000 direct manufacturing jobs in states including Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka.

learn.title: Solar Panel Types Compared
learn.intro: Choosing between monocrystalline, polycrystalline, and thin-film solar panels shapes project economics, aesthetics, and performance. Each technology converts sunlight differently, with distinct efficiency, cost, temperature, and space characteristics—making the right choice critical for rooftop, utility, building-integrated, and portable solar applications worldwide.
learn.c1_text: Monocrystalline (mono-Si) panels are made from single-crystal silicon, producing uniform black cells with the highest commercial efficiencies of 22-26%. They outperform in limited space and hot climates due to superior temperature coefficients. Premium pricing reflects the energy-intensive Czochralski crystal-growing process, but prices have fallen 90% in a decade.
learn.c2_text: Polycrystalline (poly-Si or multi-Si) panels are made by melting multiple silicon fragments together, creating the speckled blue appearance many recognize. Efficiency runs 15-20%—slightly lower than mono-Si—because grain boundaries between crystals hinder electron flow. Manufacturing is simpler and cheaper, making poly panels popular for budget residential and utility installations.
learn.c3_text: Thin-film panels deposit semiconductor layers 1-100 micrometers thick onto glass, metal, or plastic substrates. Efficiency is just 10-13%, but they excel in hot Indian conditions, perform better under partial shading, and enable flexible/BIPV applications. CdTe, CIGS, and amorphous silicon variants each suit different use cases from solar farms to rooftop shingles.
learn.stat2: Polycrystalline panels are 15-20% efficient and 20-30% cheaper than mono
learn.stat3: Thin-film efficiency typically 10-13% but degrades only 0.3% annually

learn.title: Wind Turbine End-of-Life Blade Recycling
learn.intro: Wind turbines operate 20-25 years, after which blades must be responsibly retired. With over 14,000 tonnes of blade waste expected annually by 2030, recycling is critical. Unlike steel towers and copper nacelles, composite blades resist conventional recycling, demanding innovative chemical, thermal, and mechanical recovery methods.
learn.c1_title: ♻️ Why Blades Are Hard to Recycle
learn.c1_text: Wind blades consist of fiberglass or carbon fiber embedded in epoxy or polyester resin thermoset plastics. Unlike thermoplastics, thermosets cannot be remelted. A 70-meter blade weighs 15-20 tonnes. Think of trying to recycle a surfboard crossed with rebar—strong, lightweight, and stubbornly resistant to separation without specialized chemical processes.
learn.c2_text: Three approaches are scaling commercially. Mechanical recycling shreds blades for cement co-processing. Thermal processes pyrolysis heat blades in oxygen-free chambers to recover clean fibers. Chemical solvolysis uses solvents to dissolve resin, recovering virgin-quality fibers. Companies like Vestas, Siemens Gamesa, and Carbon Rivers commercialize these techniques across Europe and the US.
learn.c3_text: India's nascent wind fleet of 47+ GW will generate blade waste from the late 2020s. Reuse options—converting blades into pedestrian bridges, bus shelters, and playground structures—are piloted by Renew Logy and Danstoker Solutions. With India targeting 140 GW of wind capacity by 2030, proactive recycling infrastructure is essential to prevent landfill accumulation.
learn.stat1: Global blade waste projected at 14,000+ tonnes annually by 2030
learn.stat2: A single 15 MW offshore blade weighs 50-70 tonnes
learn.stat3: Wind turbines operate 20-25 years before decommissioning
learn.stat4: Chemical recycling can recover up to 95% of blade materials for reuse

learn.title: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission
learn.intro: Green hydrogen—produced by electrolyzing water using renewable electricity—is emerging as a cornerstone of deep decarbonization for industry, transport, and long-duration energy storage. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to make the country a global hub, reducing import dependence on fossil fuels while enabling hard-to-abate sectors to decarbonize.
learn.c1_text: Hydrogen produced via electrolysis powered by solar or wind is classified as green. It has zero operational carbon emissions, unlike grey hydrogen from natural gas reforming. India currently consumes ~6 million tonnes of hydrogen annually, mostly grey, used in refineries and fertilizer production. Mission targets will substitute green hydrogen across these applications.
learn.c2_text: The mission targets 5 million tonnes per annum (MMTPA) of green hydrogen production by 2030, requiring 60+ GW of dedicated renewable capacity to power electrolyzers. India is incentivizing domestic electrolyzer manufacturing with INR 4,440 crore, targeting 2.5 GW of annual manufacturing capacity. PEM and alkaline electrolyzer technologies are both eligible.
learn.c3_text: The Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT) programme offers INR 13,050 crore in incentives for production and end-use deployment. Priority sectors include steel (replacing coal-based DRI), mobility (fuel-cell trucks and buses), shipping ammonia, and refineries. Pilot projects in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Kerala are testing green hydrogen in fertilizer and steel applications.
learn.stat1: India targets 5 MMTPA green hydrogen production by 2030
learn.stat3: Goal of 60 GW renewable capacity dedicated to hydrogen production
learn.stat4: Domestic electrolyzer manufacturing target: 2.5 GW per year by 2030
